micros.title: The Lakh Landmark
micros.description: Meet 1,00,000 as one lakh: how many zeros it has, where it sits on the number ladder, and where the Indian-system commas go (three digits from the right, then pairs).
outcomes: Can write 1 lakh and 10 lakh in figures with correct Indian-system commas
Can recite the landmark ladder: 1,000 -> 10,000 -> 1,00,000 -> 10,00,000

question.prompt: How is FIVE LAKH written in figures?

options.diagnosis: Wrote fifty lakh — one landmark step too far up the ladder.
Confused lakh with thousand; the landmark ladder needs rebuilding.

question.explanation: One lakh is 1,00,000 (a 1 with five zeros), so five lakh is 5,00,000. Indian commas go three digits from the right, then in pairs: 5,00,000.

micros.title: Reading and Writing 6- and 7-digit Numbers
micros.description: Read and write numbers up to ten lakh in figures and in words, using a place-value frame (TL L TTh Th H T O) and filling untouched columns with zeros.
outcomes: Can write a spoken 6- or 7-digit number in figures with every zero in place
Can read a 6- or 7-digit numeral aloud in words using lakhs and thousands

question.prompt: Write 'three lakh forty thousand six' in figures.

options.diagnosis: Pushed the 6 into the thousands block; a place-value frame keeps each spoken part in its own column.
Dropped a place — three lakh needs six more digits after the 3, with zeros holding the empty columns.

question.explanation: Fill the frame: 3 lakhs, 4 ten-thousands, 0 thousands, 0 hundreds, 0 tens, 6 ones — 3,40,006. Zeros must be written for every column that is not spoken.

micros.title: Comparing and Ordering Large Numbers
micros.description: Compare and order numbers up to ten lakh: count digits first, and only when the digit counts match, compare place by place from the left.
outcomes: Can state which of two large numbers is greater, giving digit count as the first reason
Can order four or five large numbers from smallest to greatest

question.prompt: Which number is greater: 8,76,543 or 12,34,567?

options.text: 12,34,567 — it has 7 digits while 8,76,543 has only 6
8,76,543 — because 8 is greater than 1
8,76,543 — because 76 is greater than 34
options.diagnosis: Compared inner digit pairs without lining the numbers up by place value first.

options.text: They are equal — both are in lakhs
options.diagnosis: No comparison strategy applied; digit count settles it at once.

question.explanation: Count digits first: 12,34,567 has 7 digits, so it is past ten lakh, while 8,76,543 is below ten lakh. Any 7-digit number beats any 6-digit number.

micros.title: Rounding to the Nearest Ten, Hundred and Thousand
micros.description: Round a number by finding its two neighbours at the rounding place and choosing the closer one, using the digit to the right to decide. Rounding is about closeness, not chopping.
outcomes: Can round any number to the nearest ten, hundred or thousand
Can show a rounding decision on an empty number line between the two neighbours

question.prompt: Round 45,678 to the nearest HUNDRED.

options.diagnosis: Rounded to the nearest ten; the target place was misread.
Rounded to the nearest thousand instead of the nearest hundred.

question.explanation: 45,678 sits between 45,600 and 45,700. The tens digit is 7, so 45,678 is closer to 45,700 — it rounds UP. Chopping off '78' always rounds down, which is not rounding.

micros.title: Estimating with Rounded Numbers
micros.description: Use rounded numbers to estimate sums and differences before calculating exactly, and use the estimate to sense-check the exact answer.
outcomes: Can estimate a sum or difference by rounding each number first
Can spot an unreasonable exact answer by comparing it with an estimate

micros.title: Multiplying by Tens and Hundreds (Zero Patterns)
micros.description: Multiply numbers like 60 x 400 by separating the basic fact from the zeros: do 6 x 4, then attach exactly the zeros that came from each factor.
outcomes: Can multiply by 10, 100 and their multiples using counted zeros
Can explain where each zero in the answer came from

options.diagnosis: Attached one zero too many; the zeros must be counted from the factors (1 + 2 = 3), not guessed.
Added the numbers instead of multiplying; the operation was misread.

question.explanation: 3 x 5 = 15. Now attach the zeros: one from 30 and two from 500, three in all — 15,000.

micros.title: Estimating Products and Quotients
micros.description: Round the numbers to friendly tens and hundreds to estimate a product or quotient before computing, so a wildly wrong exact answer is caught immediately.
outcomes: Can estimate a product like 245 x 32 as about 250 x 30
Can use an estimate to reject an answer that is far too big or too small

micros.title: Multiplying 3-digit by 2-digit Numbers
micros.description: Multiply a 3-digit number by a 2-digit number using partial products, writing the second row as a multiplication by tens — with its placeholder zero written first.
outcomes: Can compute a 3-digit x 2-digit product with both partial products
Can explain why the second partial-product row must end in zero

options.diagnosis: Computed 132 x 20 = 2,640 and stopped; the 132 x 4 partial product was never added.
Both partial products right (2,640 and 528) but a regrouping slip while adding them.

question.explanation: 132 x 24 = 132 x 20 + 132 x 4 = 2,640 + 528 = 3,168. Estimate first: 130 x 25 is about 3,250, so 792 is far too small — it comes from multiplying by 2 instead of 20.

micros.title: Dividing by a 2-digit Divisor
micros.description: Run long division with 2-digit divisors like 21 and 24: estimate each quotient digit by trying multiples of the divisor, then divide-multiply-subtract-bring-down as usual.
outcomes: Can divide a 3-digit number by a 2-digit divisor
Can choose a sensible first quotient digit by trying multiples of the divisor

question.prompt: 672 divided by 21 = ?

options.text: 31 remainder 21

options.diagnosis: An extra zero slipped into the quotient during bring-down; estimating (about 660 / 22 = 30) flags a 3-digit answer.
Quotient never verified — 21 x 22 = 462, leaving 210 unaccounted for; the multiply-back check is missing.

question.explanation: 21 x 32 = 672 exactly, so 672 / 21 = 32 with remainder 0. Stopping at 31 leaves remainder 21, which is as big as the divisor — one more 21 still fits.

micros.title: Checking Division: Remainder Rule and Multiply-back
micros.description: Finish every division with two checks: the remainder must be smaller than the divisor, and quotient x divisor + remainder must rebuild the dividend.
outcomes: Can verify a division answer using quotient x divisor + remainder = dividend
Can spot and fix a division that stopped with a remainder as big as the divisor

question.prompt: Asha divides 850 by 25 and writes: '33 remainder 25'. What should she notice?

options.text: The remainder 25 is not smaller than the divisor — one more 25 fits, so the answer is exactly 34
Nothing — 33 remainder 25 is a finished answer
She should add the remainder to the quotient: 33 + 25 = 58
options.diagnosis: Remainder and quotient measure different things; they can never be added together.

options.text: She must start again — 850 cannot be divided by 25
options.diagnosis: The division is possible; only the final remainder check was skipped.

question.explanation: 25 x 33 = 825, leaving 25 — but 25 fills one more whole group. So 850 / 25 = 34 exactly (25 x 34 = 850). A remainder must always be SMALLER than the divisor.

micros.title: Finding Factors with Factor Pairs
micros.description: List all factors of a number systematically by finding pairs that multiply to it (1 x 12, 2 x 6, 3 x 4), using rectangle arrays of counters as the picture.
outcomes: Can list all factors of a number up to 50 using factor pairs
Can show a factor pair as a rectangle arrangement of counters

question.prompt: Which of these is a factor of 20?

options.diagnosis: No divisibility test applied — 20 / 3 leaves remainder 2.
Used a near fact (4 x 6 = 24?); 20 / 6 leaves remainder 2, so 6 does not divide 20 exactly.

question.explanation: 5 divides 20 exactly: 5 x 4 = 20. The full factor list of 20 is 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20. Note 40 is a MULTIPLE of 20 — factors never go above the number itself.

micros.title: Multiples: The Never-ending Times Table
micros.description: List multiples of a number by skip counting, and decide whether a given number is a multiple of another by testing exact division. Multiples go on forever; factors stop at the number.
outcomes: Can list the first several multiples of any number up to 12
Can decide whether one number is a multiple of another and justify it

question.prompt: Which of these is a multiple of 6?

options.diagnosis: Looks close to the 6 times table but 26 / 6 leaves remainder 2; nearness is not divisibility.
Ends in 6, but 16 / 6 leaves remainder 4 — the last digit alone cannot decide multiples of 6.

question.explanation: 42 = 6 x 7, so 42 is a multiple of 6. The number 3 is a FACTOR of 6, not a multiple — multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24, ... and are never smaller than 6.

micros.title: Factor or Multiple? Keeping Them Apart
micros.description: Contrast the two ideas with the size rule: factors of a number fit inside it (never bigger), multiples are its times table (never smaller). Sort numbers into 'factors of n' and 'multiples of n' bins.
outcomes: Can classify given numbers as factors of n, multiples of n, or neither
Can state that n itself is both a factor and a multiple of n

question.prompt: Ravi is asked for the factors of 6 and writes: 6, 12, 18. What went wrong?

options.text: He listed multiples of 6 — the factors of 6 are 1, 2, 3 and 6
Nothing — 12 and 18 are factors of 6
Only the 6 is wrong — a number can never be its own factor
options.diagnosis: 6 IS a factor of itself (6 x 1 = 6); the wrong entries are 12 and 18.

options.text: He stopped too soon — 24 should also be in the list
options.diagnosis: Continues the multiples list; the question asked for factors, which never exceed 6.

question.explanation: Factors of 6 divide it exactly and are never bigger than 6: they are 1, 2, 3, 6. The list 6, 12, 18 is the start of the MULTIPLES of 6 — the times table of 6.

micros.title: Prime and Composite Numbers
micros.description: A prime has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. Test candidates by trying small divisors (2, 3, 5, 7), and settle the special case: 1 has only one factor, so it is neither prime nor composite.
outcomes: Can identify primes and composites up to 100 by testing small divisors
Can explain why 1 is neither prime nor composite
Can show a composite number as a rectangle array with more than one row

question.prompt: Which of these numbers is prime?

options.diagnosis: Missed 21 = 3 x 7; odd candidates must be tested against 3 and 7, not just 2.
1 has only ONE factor (itself), so it is neither prime nor composite — primes need exactly two factors.

question.explanation: 23 has exactly two factors, 1 and 23 — no number from 2 to 22 divides it. But 27 = 3 x 9 and 21 = 3 x 7: odd numbers can still be composite.

micros.title: Who Has More Factors? Size Doesn't Decide
micros.description: Count factors of several numbers and discover that bigger does not mean more factors: a small number like 12 can beat a bigger one like 25, and huge primes have only two.
outcomes: Can count and compare the number of factors of two numbers
Can give an example showing a bigger number with fewer factors

question.prompt: Which number has MORE factors: 12 or 25?

options.text: 12 — it has six factors (1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12) while 25 has only three (1, 5, 25)
25 — it is the bigger number, so it must have more factors
They have the same number — both are composite
options.diagnosis: Being composite says 'more than two factors', not 'the same count'; the lists must actually be made.

options.text: Cannot tell without dividing by every number up to 25
options.diagnosis: Factor pairs make the count quick: each divisor found brings its partner with it.

question.explanation: List them: 12 has 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 — six factors. 25 has only 1, 5, 25 — three. How many factors a number has depends on how it is built, not on how big it is.

micros.title: Making Equivalent Fractions
micros.description: Generate fractions that name the same amount by multiplying BOTH the numerator and denominator by the same number — re-cutting every piece into equal sub-pieces on a fraction wall.
outcomes: Can generate equivalent fractions by multiplying both terms by the same number
Can explain with a picture why multiplying both terms keeps the amount unchanged

question.prompt: Which fraction is equivalent to 2/5?

options.diagnosis: Doubled only the denominator — that halves the fraction instead of preserving it.
Doubled only the numerator — that doubles the fraction; both terms must change together.

question.explanation: Multiply top and bottom by the same number: 2/5 = (2x2)/(5x2) = 4/10. Adding 1 to both terms gives 3/6, which equals 1/2 — a different amount. Check both on a fraction wall.

micros.title: Reducing to Simplest Form
micros.description: Run equivalence backwards: divide both terms by the same number until no common divisor is left, giving the fraction in its simplest form.
outcomes: Can reduce a fraction like 6/8 to its simplest form
Can check that a fraction is fully simplified by hunting for common divisors

question.prompt: What is 6/8 in its simplest form?

options.diagnosis: Subtracted 2 from both terms — additive change moves the amount (4/6 = 2/3, not 6/8).
Swapped numerator and denominator; flipping a fraction changes its value completely.

question.explanation: Divide both terms by 2: 6/8 = 3/4, and 3 and 4 share no common divisor, so it is fully simplified. Subtracting 1 from both terms gives 5/7 — a different point on the number line.

micros.title: Comparing with Same Denominators or Same Numerators
micros.description: Two quick comparison rules: same denominator — more pieces wins; same numerator — the bigger denominator means smaller pieces, so it LOSES.
outcomes: Can compare fractions with equal denominators by comparing numerators
Can compare fractions with equal numerators by reasoning about piece size

question.prompt: Which is greater: 3/5 or 3/8?

options.text: 3/5 — fifths are bigger pieces than eighths, and there are 3 of each
3/8 — because 8 is greater than 5
They are equal — both have numerator 3
options.diagnosis: Compared numerators only; the denominators say how big each piece is.

options.text: They cannot be compared without a common denominator
options.diagnosis: Common denominators always work, but same-numerator reasoning settles this instantly.

question.explanation: Both take 3 pieces, but a fifth of a roti is bigger than an eighth of it. So 3/5 > 3/8. (Common denominators agree: 24/40 > 15/40.)

micros.title: Comparing Any Two Fractions with a Common Denominator
micros.description: When neither the tops nor the bottoms match, rewrite both fractions with a common denominator using equivalence, then compare the numerators.
outcomes: Can compare two unlike fractions by rewriting both over a common denominator
Can pick a sensible common denominator for a pair of fractions

question.prompt: Which is greater: 2/3 or 3/5?

options.text: 2/3 — as fifteenths, 2/3 = 10/15 and 3/5 = 9/15
3/5 — because 5 is greater than 3, fifths beat thirds
3/5 — because 3 is greater than 2 on top
options.diagnosis: Compared numerators of fractions with DIFFERENT denominators; the pieces are not the same size.

options.text: They are equal — 2/3 becomes 3/5 by adding 1 to top and bottom

question.explanation: Rewrite both over 15: 2/3 = 10/15 and 3/5 = 9/15, so 2/3 is greater. Adding 1 to both terms does NOT keep a fraction equal — it slides it to a new point.

micros.title: Benchmark Tricks: Half and Distance from One Whole
micros.description: Compare fractions mentally against benchmarks: is each more or less than 1/2? For near-whole fractions like 5/6 and 7/8, compare the SIZE of the missing piece instead of the count.
outcomes: Can decide whether a fraction is more or less than 1/2 without computing
Can compare near-whole fractions by comparing their distances from 1

question.prompt: Which is greater: 7/8 or 9/10?

options.text: 9/10 — it is missing only 1/10, and 1/10 is smaller than the missing 1/8
They are equal — each is exactly one piece short of a whole
7/8 — eighths are bigger pieces than tenths
options.diagnosis: Right fact, wrong conclusion — bigger pieces make the MISSING piece bigger too, pulling 7/8 further below 1.

options.text: Cannot say without a calculator
options.diagnosis: Distance-from-one settles it mentally: compare the missing pieces 1/8 and 1/10.

micros.title: Adding and Subtracting Like Fractions
micros.description: With the same denominator, only the counts of pieces are added or subtracted — the denominator is the NAME of the piece and stays put: 3 eighths + 2 eighths = 5 eighths.
outcomes: Can add and subtract fractions with the same denominator
Can explain why the denominator does not change during the operation

options.diagnosis: Multiplied the numerators (2 x 3 = 6); a times-table fact intruded on addition.
Subtracted the numerators — the operation sign was misread.

question.explanation: 2 sevenths + 3 sevenths = 5 sevenths = 5/7. The denominator is the piece's name — it never gets added, just as 2 mangoes + 3 mangoes is 5 mangoes.

micros.title: Adding with Related Denominators
micros.description: When one denominator is a multiple of the other (halves and quarters, thirds and sixths), first re-cut the coarser fraction into the finer pieces using equivalence, then add like fractions.
outcomes: Can add fractions where one denominator is a multiple of the other
Can write and verify the renaming step (1/2 = 2/4) before adding

options.diagnosis: Subtracted instead of adding: 1/3 - 1/6 = 1/6; the operation sign was misread.

question.explanation: Re-cut the third into sixths: 1/3 = 2/6. Then 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6 = 1/2. Changing only the denominator (1/3 into 1/6) silently shrinks the fraction — the numerator must scale too.

micros.title: Subtracting with Related Denominators
micros.description: Subtract fractions like 3/4 - 1/8 by first renaming the coarser fraction into the finer pieces (3/4 = 6/8), then subtracting the counts.
outcomes: Can subtract fractions where one denominator is a multiple of the other
Can check a fraction subtraction by adding back

micros.title: Taking a Fraction Away from a Whole
micros.description: Rename 1 as 4/4, 8/8 or whatever denominator is needed — the same whole in different clothes — so that fractions can be subtracted from wholes.
outcomes: Can rewrite 1 (or 2, 3, ...) as an equivalent fraction with any denominator
Can subtract a fraction from a whole number

question.prompt: A water tank is full. The family uses 2/5 of it in one day. How much of the tank is left?

options.text: It cannot be worked out — you cannot take 2/5 away from 1

options.diagnosis: Reported the part USED; the question asks for the part remaining.
Added instead of subtracting; using water removes it from the whole.

question.explanation: Rename the full tank: 1 = 5/5. Then 5/5 - 2/5 = 3/5 of the tank is left. Any whole can be rewritten as a fraction over the denominator you need.

micros.title: Fraction Word Problems: Food, Time and Lengths
micros.description: Solve one-step story problems about sharing food, cooking measures, time and lengths by choosing add or subtract, renaming where needed, and sanity-checking the answer against the whole.
outcomes: Can translate a one-step fraction story into an addition or subtraction
Can judge whether a fraction answer is sensible (not bigger than the whole, etc.)

question.prompt: A recipe needs 1/2 cup of dal plus 1/4 cup extra. How much dal is that in all?

options.text: 3/4 cup
2/6 cup
2/4 cup
1/8 cup
options.diagnosis: Multiplied the fractions instead of adding them; 'plus extra' means addition.

question.explanation: Re-cut the half into quarters: 1/2 = 2/4. Then 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4 cup. Adding tops and bottoms (2/6) gives less than the 1/2 cup you started with — impossible when you are adding more.

micros.title: Tenths on the Number Line
micros.description: Cut the gap between whole numbers into ten equal hops: each hop is one tenth, written 0.1. Read and place numbers like 0.4 and 2.7 on the number line and connect them to fractions like 4/10.
outcomes: Can write tenths as both fractions (7/10) and decimals (0.7)
Can place and read tenths on a number line between whole numbers

question.prompt: On a number line, each hop from 0 is one tenth. What number do you reach after 4 hops?

options.diagnosis: Landed in the hundredths column; one hop of a tenth is 0.1, not 0.01.
Glued the count and the denominator together; the 10 is shown by the digit's POSITION, not written out.

question.explanation: Four hops of one tenth is 4 tenths = 4/10 = 0.4 — still less than 1. Reaching the number 4 would take forty hops.

micros.title: Hundredths and Money
micros.description: Split each tenth into ten again to get hundredths: 0.07 is 7/100, ten times smaller than 0.7. Money makes it concrete — 1 rupee is 100 paise, so 45 paise is Rs 0.45.
outcomes: Can write hundredths as fractions and decimals and tell them apart from tenths
Can convert between rupees-and-paise and decimal rupee amounts

question.prompt: 1 rupee = 100 paise. How do you write 45 paise in rupees?

options.text: Rs 45

options.diagnosis: Wrote 45 TENTHS of a rupee — that is 4 rupees 50 paise, ten times too much.
Slid the digits one place too far; 45 out of 100 sits in the tenths and hundredths columns.

question.explanation: 45 paise is 45 out of 100 paise, so it is 45/100 of a rupee = Rs 0.45. Dropping the decimal point turns 45 paise into 45 whole rupees — a hundred times too much.

micros.title: Extending the Place-value Table Past the Point
micros.description: Add tenths and hundredths columns to the right of the ones: each step right divides by 10. Name every digit by its column, and see why 0.30 equals 0.3 but 0.03 does not.
outcomes: Can state the place value of any digit in a number like 3.65
Can explain why a zero at the right end after the point changes nothing

question.prompt: In the number 3.65, what is the value of the digit 6?

options.text: 6 tenths (0.6)
just 6
6 hundredths (0.06)
options.diagnosis: Counted one column too far right; the first place after the point is tenths.
Read the digits 65 as a whole number sitting after the 3; the point pins each digit to a column.

question.explanation: The first column after the decimal point is tenths, so the 6 in 3.65 is worth 6 tenths = 0.6. The 5 next to it is 5 hundredths.

micros.title: Comparing Decimals Place by Place
micros.description: Compare decimals by lining up the places and comparing from the left, padding with zeros so both have the same number of places — never by counting digits.
outcomes: Can compare two decimals by padding to equal places and comparing place by place
Can order a mixed list like 0.5, 0.45, 0.7 from smallest to largest

question.prompt: Which is greater: 0.6 or 0.42?

options.text: 0.6 — it equals 0.60, and 60 hundredths is more than 42 hundredths
0.42 — because 42 is greater than 6
0.42 — more decimal places always make a bigger number
options.diagnosis: Digit COUNT is being used instead of place value; extra places refine a number, they do not enlarge it.

options.text: They are equal — both start with 0
options.diagnosis: Compared only the whole-number parts and stopped; the tenths digits (6 vs 4) decide it.

question.explanation: Pad to equal places: 0.6 = 0.60. Comparing tenths first: 6 tenths beats 4 tenths, so 0.6 > 0.42. On a hundred-square grid, 0.6 shades 60 small squares and 0.42 only 42.

micros.title: Decimals and Fractions: Two Names, One Number
micros.description: Translate both ways between decimals and fractions with denominators 10 and 100 (0.25 = 25/100 = 1/4), and place both forms at the same point on the number line.
outcomes: Can convert tenths and hundredths between fraction and decimal form both ways
Can show that a decimal and its fraction sit at the same point on the number line

question.prompt: Which fraction is exactly equal to 0.25?

options.diagnosis: Used the digits 2 and 5 as top and bottom; 2/5 = 0.4, a different number.
Turned the digits into a denominator; 0.25 means 25 parts OF a hundred, not 1 part of 25.

question.explanation: Two places after the point means hundredths: 0.25 = 25/100, which simplifies to 1/4. Writing 25/10 would be 25 tenths = 2.5 — the point's position matters.

micros.title: Lining Up the Decimal Points
micros.description: Set up decimal additions in columns with the decimal points in one vertical line, padding ragged numbers with trailing zeros (4.5 becomes 4.50) so every column is complete.
outcomes: Can set up and add decimals with different numbers of places correctly
Can explain why right-aligning the digits (ignoring the points) gives wrong answers

options.diagnosis: Shifted 3.2 one column over (added 3.2 to 14.5); the points must sit in one vertical line.
Dropped the 5 hundredths; padding 3.2 to 3.20 keeps every column accounted for.

question.explanation: Line up the points and pad: 3.20 + 1.45. Hundredths: 0 + 5 = 5; tenths: 2 + 4 = 6; ones: 3 + 1 = 4. Answer: 4.65. Right-aligning the raw digits computes 32 + 145 and lands on 1.77.

micros.title: Carrying Across the Decimal Point
micros.description: See the carry cross the point: 8 tenths + 6 tenths = 14 tenths = 1 whole and 4 tenths. The point separates columns, not two different numbers.
outcomes: Can add decimals where tenths regroup into ones (and hundredths into tenths)
Can explain a carry across the point using tenths language

options.diagnosis: Lost the decimal point entirely and answered in whole numbers.
Addition-fact slip (7 + 5 taken as 13); the decimal handling itself is right.

question.explanation: 7 tenths + 5 tenths = 12 tenths = 1 whole and 2 tenths = 1.2. Writing 0.12 traps the 12 after the point — ten of those tenths must carry into the ones.

micros.title: Subtracting Decimals with Borrowing
micros.description: Subtract decimals in columns, padding with zeros (6 becomes 6.00) so borrows can visibly cross the decimal point, and check by adding back or counting up.
outcomes: Can subtract decimals including borrows that cross the decimal point
Can check a decimal subtraction by counting up from the smaller number

options.diagnosis: A single borrow slip in the tenths column; the overall method is intact.
Borrowed from the ones twice; write 6 as 6.00 and track each borrow once.

question.explanation: Write 6 as 6.00, then subtract: 6.00 - 2.75 = 3.25. Check by counting up: 2.75 + 0.25 = 3, and 3 + 3 = 6, so the gap is 3.25. Doing '6 - 2 = 4, keep the .75' counts the 75 hundredths the wrong way.

micros.title: Bills and Change with Money
micros.description: Total a shopping bill in rupees and paise and work out the change from a note, using column work or the shopkeeper's counting-up method.
outcomes: Can total a bill of two or three decimal money amounts
Can compute change from a note, borrowing across the point correctly

question.prompt: Arun's bill at the kirana shop is Rs 63.50. He pays with a Rs 100 note. How much change should he get?

options.diagnosis: A borrow slip in the tens column; estimate first — the change should be a bit less than 40.
Reported the bill instead of the change; the subtraction from 100 was never done.

question.explanation: 100.00 - 63.50 = 36.50. Count up to check: 63.50 + 0.50 = 64, and 64 + 36 = 100, so the change is Rs 36.50. The shortcut '100 - 63 = 37, keep the .50' double-counts the 50 paise.

micros.title: Adding and Subtracting Measures
micros.description: Apply decimal addition and subtraction to real measures — race timings in seconds, weights in kilograms, lengths in metres — keeping units consistent throughout.
outcomes: Can add and subtract decimal measurements of length, weight and time
Can state the answer with its correct unit

micros.title: An Angle Is a Turn
micros.description: An angle measures how far one arm swings away from the other — the opening, not the drawing. Longer arms do not make a bigger angle.
outcomes: Can compare two angles by their openings, ignoring arm length
Can demonstrate an angle as a turn with arms, scissors or clock hands

question.prompt: Angle P is drawn with arms 10 cm long but a narrow opening. Angle Q has arms only 3 cm long but is opened much wider. Which angle is bigger?

options.text: Angle Q — the angle is the amount of opening between the arms
Angle P — its arms are much longer
They are equal — both have two arms
options.diagnosis: Counting arms tells you it IS an angle; the amount of turn between them is what is measured.

options.text: Impossible to compare without a protractor
options.diagnosis: Wide-versus-narrow can be compared by overlaying tracings; no measuring is needed.

question.explanation: An angle measures the TURN between its arms. Extending or shortening the arms changes the picture's size, not the opening. Q is opened wider, so Q is the bigger angle.

micros.title: Right Angles in Every Direction
micros.description: Make a folded-paper corner tester and use it to find right angles around you — including tilted ones. The tester fits or it doesn't; the tilt is irrelevant.
outcomes: Can test any corner for a right angle with a folded-paper tester
Can recognise right angles in non-standard orientations

question.prompt: A kite's corner is a right angle, but the kite hangs tilted so neither arm is horizontal or vertical. Is the corner still a right angle?

options.text: Yes — tilting the whole corner does not change how open it is
No — a right angle needs one flat arm and one upright arm
No — tilting squeezes it into an acute angle
options.diagnosis: Rotation moves both arms together; the opening between them never changes.

options.text: Only if you redraw it on squared paper
options.diagnosis: An angle's size belongs to the angle, not to the paper beneath it.

question.explanation: A folded-paper corner tester still fits the kite's corner perfectly however it hangs. Turning an angle moves both arms together, so the 90-degree opening is unchanged.

micros.title: Degree Landmarks: 90, 180, 360
micros.description: Anchor the three big degree landmarks with body turns and the clock: a quarter turn is 90 (right angle), a half turn is 180 (straight angle), a full spin is 360.
outcomes: Can state the degrees in a right angle, straight angle and full turn
Can show that four square corners fill a full turn (4 x 90 = 360)

question.prompt: How many degrees are there in a FULL turn (spinning all the way around)?

options.diagnosis: Degrees do not work in hundreds like money; a full turn is four right angles, 4 x 90 = 360.
Named the quarter turn (right angle); a full spin is four of those.

question.explanation: Face north and spin all the way back to north: that is 360 degrees. Half way (facing south) is 180, and a quarter (facing east) is 90 — four square corners tile a full turn.

micros.title: Acute, Right, Obtuse, Straight
micros.description: Classify angles against the 90-degree benchmark: smaller than a right angle is acute, bigger (but less than straight) is obtuse. Use the corner tester as the judge.
outcomes: Can classify a drawn angle as acute, right, obtuse or straight
Can find one angle of each type in the classroom

question.prompt: An angle measures 120 degrees. What kind of angle is it?

options.text: Obtuse — bigger than 90 but less than 180
Acute
options.diagnosis: Acute means SMALLER than a right angle; 120 is past the 90 benchmark.

options.text: Right
options.diagnosis: A right angle is exactly 90; 120 overshoots it by 30.

options.text: Straight
options.diagnosis: A straight angle is exactly 180 — a full straight line; 120 is short of that.

question.explanation: Compare with the landmarks: 90 < 120 < 180, so the angle is obtuse — wider than a square corner but not yet a straight line.

micros.title: Estimating Everyday Angles
micros.description: Estimate the angles made by clock hands, door openings, scissors and laptop lids by comparing them with the 90-degree benchmark and its half, 45.
outcomes: Can estimate a real-world angle to the nearest landmark (45, 90, 180)
Can state the angle between clock hands at o'clock times like 3:00 and 6:00

question.prompt: At exactly 3:00, what angle do the clock's two hands make?

options.text: 90 degrees — a right angle, a quarter of the clock face
180 degrees
15 degrees
options.diagnosis: Counted the 15 minutes between the hands; minutes are not degrees — 15 minutes is a quarter of the face, which is 90 degrees.

options.text: 3 degrees
options.diagnosis: Read the hour number as the angle; the angle comes from the turn between the hands.

question.explanation: At 3:00 the hands point to 12 and 3 — a quarter of the way around the face. A quarter of the full 360 is 90 degrees, a perfect right angle. (6:00 gives the straight 180.)

micros.title: Faces, Edges and Vertices of Boxes
micros.description: Count the 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices of cubes and cuboids using real boxes and paint-stamping, remembering that a drawing hides half the faces.
outcomes: Can count faces, edges and vertices of cubes and cuboids, including hidden ones
Can mark the hidden faces on a sketch of a box

question.prompt: How many faces does a closed cuboid box (like a toothpaste carton) have?

options.diagnosis: Counted the edges instead of the faces.
Counted the corners (vertices) instead of the faces.

question.explanation: Every cuboid has 6 faces: top, bottom, front, back and two sides. A drawing can only show 3 of them — stamp each face of a real box in paint and you always get 6 prints.

micros.title: Will It Fold into a Cube?
micros.description: Test arrangements of six squares by real and mental folding. Six squares are necessary but not enough — the ARRANGEMENT decides whether it closes into a cube.
outcomes: Can decide by folding (mental or paper) whether a 6-square arrangement is a cube net
Can explain why a 1x6 strip and a 2x3 block fail as cube nets

question.prompt: Six squares are joined in a 2 x 3 block (two rows of three). Will this fold into a cube?

options.text: No — folding makes squares land on top of each other, leaving some faces uncovered
Yes — it has exactly 6 squares, which is all a cube needs
Yes — any six squares work if you fold gently
options.diagnosis: No folding test was performed; care cannot fix an impossible layout.

options.text: No — a cube's net needs 8 squares
options.diagnosis: Wrong face count; a cube needs 6 squares — the 2 x 3 block fails because of its arrangement.

question.explanation: Fold the 2 x 3 block and squares overlap while two faces of the cube stay open. Six squares are needed, but only 11 special arrangements fold into a cube — count and layout both matter.

micros.title: Many Nets, One Box
micros.description: Unfold identical boxes along different edges to collect different-looking nets of the same cube — cross, T and Z shapes are all valid. A net records the unfolding path, not the solid's silhouette.
outcomes: Can accept and verify unfamiliar-looking valid cube nets
Can produce two different nets of the same box by unfolding along different edges

question.prompt: A net is drawn as a cross: a column of four squares, with one square attached to each side of the second square. Can it fold into a cube?

options.text: Yes — the four column squares wrap around, and the two side squares close the ends
No — a cube is square-shaped, and this looks like a plus sign
No — only a 2 x 3 rectangle of squares folds into a cube
options.diagnosis: Reversed: the compact 2 x 3 block is one of the arrangements that FAILS; the cross is a classic valid net.

options.text: Only if the cross is drawn upright
options.diagnosis: Rotating a net changes nothing about how it folds.

question.explanation: Fold the column of four into a ring (front, bottom, back, top), then the two side squares swing up to become the left and right faces. A net never looks like the solid — it records an unfolding.

micros.title: Opposite Faces on a Net
micros.description: Predict which faces of a net end up opposite each other after folding, and check with a dice — opposite faces of a dice always add up to 7.
outcomes: Can mark pairs of opposite faces on a cube net before folding
Can use the opposite-faces-sum-to-7 rule of a dice

micros.title: Drawing Nets and Box Sketches
micros.description: Draw a correct net for an open or closed box and make a simple 3D sketch of a box on flat paper, choosing the right number of faces for each design.
outcomes: Can draw a net for a closed box (6 faces) and an open box (5 faces)
Can sketch a cuboid showing its hidden edges with dotted lines

question.prompt: You are drawing the net for a CLOSED cuboid gift box. How many rectangle faces must the net contain?

options.diagnosis: Left out the lid — 5 faces is the net of an OPEN box, but this one is closed.
Counted edges instead of faces; the net needs one rectangle per face.

question.explanation: A closed box has 6 faces, so its net needs all 6 rectangles — including the bottom and back you cannot see in a sketch. An open box would need only 5.

micros.title: Quarter, Half and Full Turns
micros.description: Connect turn words to degrees and directions: a quarter turn is 90, a half turn 180, a full turn 360 — and turns add up, so two quarter turns make a half turn.
outcomes: Can state the degrees for quarter, half and full turns
Can combine turns (two quarters make a half; four quarters return home)

question.prompt: Riya makes two quarter turns in the same direction. How far has she turned in all?

options.text: A half turn — 180 degrees
A full turn — she is back where she started
A quarter turn — 90 degrees
options.diagnosis: Each new turn was treated as starting over; turns in the same direction add up.

options.text: 45 degrees
options.diagnosis: Halved a quarter turn instead of doubling it; 90 + 90 = 180.

question.explanation: Each quarter turn is 90 degrees, so two of them make 90 + 90 = 180 — a half turn. Facing north, Riya now faces south. It takes FOUR quarter turns to get back to the start.

micros.title: Predicting a Shape After a Turn
micros.description: Predict what a letter or shape looks like after a quarter or half turn using trace-and-turn: trace it, pin the centre, rotate the tracing. Turning is spinning flat — not flipping over.
outcomes: Can draw or pick the image of a shape after a 90 or 180 degree turn
Can distinguish the result of a turn from the result of a mirror flip

question.prompt: Which of these letters looks EXACTLY the same after a half turn (180 degrees)?

options.text: N
E — it is symmetric, so it must look the same
A — it is balanced, so it looks the same upside down
b — every letter survives a half turn
options.diagnosis: Turn it and check: b spins into q; trace-and-turn is the test, not a guess.

question.explanation: Trace N, pin its centre and spin it 180 degrees: it lands exactly on itself. E has a MIRROR line but spins into a backwards E; A turns upside down; b becomes q. Mirror symmetry and turning symmetry are different tests.

micros.title: The Trace-and-Turn Symmetry Test
micros.description: Test whether a figure has turning symmetry: trace it, rotate the tracing a quarter or half turn, and see if it truly matches — and notice this is independent of mirror symmetry.
outcomes: Can test a figure for quarter-turn and half-turn symmetry with a tracing
Can give an example with turning symmetry but no mirror line (like S), and the reverse

question.prompt: The letter S has no mirror line at all. Does it look the same after a half turn?

options.text: Yes — spin S half way around and it lands exactly on itself
No — without a line of symmetry it cannot have turning symmetry
No — it becomes the number 2
options.diagnosis: That is what a mirror FLIP does to S; a flat spin keeps its curves hooked the same way.

options.text: Only shapes with straight sides can have turning symmetry
options.diagnosis: Curved figures can have turning symmetry too — test with a tracing, not a rule about sides.

question.explanation: Trace S, pin the centre and rotate 180 degrees: it matches itself perfectly. Mirror symmetry and turning symmetry are separate properties — S has the second without the first.

micros.title: Patterns Built from Turns
micros.description: Continue and create border and tiling patterns made by repeating one motif with a quarter or half turn each time, as in rangoli and railway-station floors.
outcomes: Can continue a border pattern whose rule is 'turn the motif 90 degrees each time'
Can design a four-tile motif pattern using repeated quarter turns

micros.title: Area Formula from Rows of Squares
micros.description: Turn square-counting into multiplication: a rectangle's unit squares sit in equal rows, so area = length x width. The formula is a fast way of counting squares, and its unit is SQUARE units.
outcomes: Can compute a rectangle's area with length x width and justify it with rows
Can attach square units (sq cm, sq m) to every area answer

question.prompt: A rectangle is 7 cm long and 3 cm wide. What is its AREA?

options.text: 21 square cm
20 square cm
21 cm
10 square cm
options.diagnosis: Added the two sides (7 + 3) instead of multiplying the rows of squares.

question.explanation: Area = 7 x 3 = 21 square cm — three rows of seven unit squares. 20 comes from the perimeter recipe 2 x (7 + 3); and area must carry SQUARE units because it counts squares, not sticks.

micros.title: Perimeter Formula: 2 x (Length + Width)
micros.description: Walk the boundary — long, short, long, short — and compress it into the shortcut perimeter = 2 x (length + width), measured in plain length units.
outcomes: Can compute a rectangle's perimeter with 2 x (length + width)
Can explain the formula as walking all four sides

question.prompt: A rectangular garden is 10 m long and 6 m wide. How much fencing does its PERIMETER need?

options.diagnosis: Computed length + width but forgot to double — only half the boundary was walked.
Doubled only the length (2 x 10 + 6); both widths must be counted too.

question.explanation: Perimeter = 2 x (10 + 6) = 2 x 16 = 32 m. Multiplying 10 x 6 = 60 gives the AREA in square metres — the grass inside, not the fence around it.

micros.title: Cover It or Go Around It? Choosing Formula and Unit
micros.description: Sort real problems by the question they ask — covering (area, square units) or surrounding (perimeter, length units) — before touching any numbers.
outcomes: Can decide whether a word problem needs area or perimeter
Can pick the correct unit (cm vs sq cm, m vs sq m) for each answer

question.prompt: You want to know how much carpet covers a room's floor. Which unit should the answer be in?

options.text: Square metres — carpet covers a surface
Metres
Cubic metres
options.diagnosis: Cubic units measure filled SPACE (volume); a carpet covers a flat surface.

options.text: Litres
options.diagnosis: Litres measure liquid capacity; a floor is covered, not filled.

question.explanation: Covering questions are area questions, and area is measured by laying down unit SQUARES — so square metres. Plain metres would measure the skirting that runs AROUND the room (perimeter).

micros.title: Finding a Missing Side
micros.description: Run the formulas backwards: given a rectangle's area (or perimeter) and one side, find the other side by dividing (or halving then subtracting).
outcomes: Can find a missing side from the area and one side
Can find a missing side from the perimeter and one side

question.prompt: A rectangle has an AREA of 24 square cm. Its length is 6 cm. What is its width?

options.text: 4 cm
6 cm
18 cm
options.diagnosis: Subtracted 6 from 24; area is length TIMES width, so undoing it needs division.

options.text: 144 cm
options.diagnosis: Multiplied 24 by 6 instead of dividing; check — a 6 x 144 rectangle has a huge area, not 24.

question.explanation: Area = length x width, so width = 24 / 6 = 4 cm. Check: 6 x 4 = 24 square cm. Answering 6 comes from treating 24 as the PERIMETER: 2 x (6 + 6) = 24 — the wrong formula.

micros.title: Same Fence, Different Fields
micros.description: Explore rectangles sharing one perimeter and discover their areas differ — the squarer the rectangle, the more it encloses. Equal boundary never guarantees equal area.
outcomes: Can build several rectangles with the same perimeter and compute each area
Can explain why a fixed fence length can enclose different amounts of ground

question.prompt: Two plots each use exactly 20 m of fencing: Plot A is 2 m x 8 m and Plot B is 5 m x 5 m. Do they enclose the same area?

options.text: No — Plot B holds 25 sq m but Plot A only 16 sq m
Yes — the same fence means the same space inside
Plot A is bigger — it is longer
options.diagnosis: One long dimension does not decide coverage; the narrow 2 m width starves Plot A of area.

options.text: They cannot be compared without walking around both
options.diagnosis: The formulas settle it: 2 x 8 = 16 and 5 x 5 = 25 square metres.

question.explanation: Both perimeters are 20 m (2 x (2+8) = 20 and 4 x 5 = 20), but the areas are 16 and 25 square metres. Same fence, different fields — the squarer plot is roomier.

micros.title: Volume Is Counting Cubes
micros.description: Volume measures filled space, and its unit is a little cube — not a flat square. Find the volume of small cube buildings by counting every unit cube.
outcomes: Can find the volume of a simple cube building by counting unit cubes
Can state that volume is measured in cubes while area is measured in squares

micros.title: X-ray Counting: The Hidden Cubes
micros.description: Drawings hide cubes at the back and underneath, but they still count. Practise X-ray counting: for each visible column, count how many cubes stand in it top to bottom.
outcomes: Can count all cubes in a drawn stack, including hidden ones
Can verify a drawing count by building the solid from real cubes

question.prompt: A solid stack is 3 cubes long, 2 cubes wide and 2 cubes high. In the drawing, Ravi can see only 9 cubes, so he answers 9. How many cubes are really in the stack?

options.diagnosis: Counted only the front layer plus one; a 3-wide, 2-deep, 2-high block has two full layers of six.
Multiplied the wrong dimensions (perhaps 4 x 4); the block is 3 x 2 x 2.

question.explanation: Each layer holds 3 x 2 = 6 cubes, and there are 2 layers: 6 x 2 = 12. The cubes hidden at the back and bottom of the drawing are still there — a drawing shows at most three sides.

micros.title: Counting by Layers
micros.description: A box packs cubes in identical layers, so the fast count is cubes in one layer x number of layers — watched live by filling a real box layer by layer.
outcomes: Can compute a box's cube count as one layer x layers
Can find the cubes in one layer as rows x columns

question.prompt: A carton is filled with 3 layers of cubes. Each layer has 4 rows of 3 cubes. How many cubes fill the carton?

options.diagnosis: Added rows and columns first (4 + 3 = 7) then multiplied by layers; one layer holds 4 x 3 = 12 cubes.
Added all three numbers (4 + 3 + 3); the structure is layers OF arrays, which multiply.

question.explanation: One layer holds 4 x 3 = 12 cubes. Three layers hold 12 x 3 = 36 cubes. Stopping at 12 counts only the bottom layer — the box keeps filling upward.

micros.title: Rearranging Never Changes Volume
micros.description: Rebuild the same set of cubes from a tall tower into a flat slab and back: the shape changes, the count never does. Height and spread trade off; nothing is created or destroyed.
outcomes: Can state that rearranging cubes preserves volume, with a demonstration
Can reject 'taller means more' by counting both builds

question.prompt: Meena stacks 18 cubes into one tall tower. Arjun arranges his own 18 identical cubes into a low 3 x 3 x 2 block. Whose build takes up more space?

options.text: Both the same — 18 cubes is 18 cubes, however they are arranged
Meena's — the tower is taller, so it must be more
Impossible to tell without weighing both builds
Arjun's — his block covers more of the table
options.diagnosis: Judged by footprint; spreading out is the flip side of height, and neither changes the cube count.

question.explanation: Check Arjun's block: 3 x 3 x 2 = 18 cubes — exactly Meena's count. Rearranging never adds or removes a cube, so the volumes are equal. Weighing would only confirm 18 = 18.

micros.title: Comparing and Ordering Volumes
micros.description: Compare cube buildings by count (not by look) and order containers by how much they hold, previewing capacity: pouring and packing decide, not height alone.
outcomes: Can compare two cube buildings by computing both volumes
Can order three containers or builds from smallest to largest volume

micros.title: Reading Data Tables
micros.description: Pull the right value out of a table, then compare entries to find least and greatest — routing every comparison through place value, not first digits.
outcomes: Can extract a named value from a data table
Can find the least and greatest entries in a table column correctly

question.prompt: A table shows rainfall in mm: June 8, July 12, August 25, September 9. Which month had the MOST rain?

options.text: August
September — 9 is the biggest digit in the list
June
options.diagnosis: Picked the least value — the question asks for the most; flag least/most words before reading.

options.text: July
options.diagnosis: Compared 12 and 25 by their second digits; line values up and compare place by place from the left.

question.explanation: Compare all four: 8 < 9 < 12 < 25, so August (25 mm) had the most rain. A big single digit like 9 still loses to any two-digit number.

micros.title: Bar Graphs with Scaled Axes
micros.description: Read bar graphs where one division stands for 5, 10 or more: run the scale-check ritual first, and read bars that end between gridlines exactly — the half division is data too.
outcomes: Can state a bar graph's scale before reading any bar
Can read a bar ending mid-division as divisions x scale, including the half

question.prompt: On a runs-per-over graph, 1 division stands for 10 runs. The bar for over 3 rises 3 and a half divisions. How many runs were scored in over 3?

options.diagnosis: Multiplied by the scale but dropped the half division — that half stands for 5 real runs.
Rounded the bar up to the next gridline before scaling; the graph must be read exactly.

question.explanation: 3.5 divisions x 10 runs per division = 35 runs. Counting gridlines as if each were 1 (and rounding the half away) throws away both the scale and part of the data.

micros.title: Pie Slices Are Fractions of the Total
micros.description: Read a simple pie chart by writing the total above it first, then computing each slice as a fraction OF that total: half of 80 is 40, a quarter of 80 is 20.
outcomes: Can compute the count for a half or quarter slice from the stated total
Can explain why the same slice means different counts for different totals

question.prompt: A pie chart shows the favourite games of 80 children. The cricket slice is a QUARTER of the circle. How many children chose cricket?

options.diagnosis: Took half of 80 instead of a quarter; the slice is one fourth of the circle.
Used the denominator of the fraction as the answer; the quarter must be applied TO the total of 80.

question.explanation: A quarter OF the 80 children is 80 / 4 = 20. The answer 25 treats 'quarter' as a fixed number (like 25 out of 100), but a slice is a fraction whose count depends on the total.

micros.title: Comparing Pie Charts with Different Totals
micros.description: Compare slices across two pie charts with different totals and discover that a smaller slice of a bigger total can beat a bigger slice of a smaller total.
outcomes: Can compare slice counts across two pies by applying each fraction to its own total
Can explain why slice size alone cannot be compared across pies

question.prompt: In School A's pie chart (100 students), HALF the circle likes mango. In School B's pie chart (400 students), only a QUARTER of the circle likes mango. Which school has more mango lovers?

options.text: School B — a quarter of 400 is 100, more than half of 100, which is 50
School A — half a circle always beats a quarter circle
They are equal — the slices balance out
options.diagnosis: No computation done; each fraction must be applied to its OWN total before comparing.

options.text: Cannot be answered from pie charts
options.diagnosis: It can — the totals are given, so each slice converts to a real count.

question.explanation: Half of 100 = 50 mango lovers at School A; a quarter of 400 = 100 at School B. The smaller-looking slice wins because its total is four times bigger — a slice is a fraction, not a count.

micros.title: Multi-step Questions from One Display
micros.description: Answer questions that need two or more readings from the same table or graph — totals across rows, differences between bars, and 'how many more' comparisons.
outcomes: Can combine two readings from one display into a total or difference
Can answer 'how many more' questions from tables and bar graphs
